Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in Microsoft.Native.Quic.MsQuic.Schannel. This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability.

Various vulnerabilities in MsQuic are addressed by an updated native-binary dependency update.

Announcement

  • Score: 5.9

  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:H/I:N/A:N

Affected Platforms

  • Architectures: All

items.content_html:
Impact

MessagePack-CSharp is vulnerable to denial of service through excessive memory allocation when deserializing attacker-controlled data into System.Object.

When PrimitiveObjectFormatter encounters an array, it allocates an object[] using the declared array length before enforcing the configured maximum object-graph depth. A specially crafted payload containing deeply nested arrays can therefore keep many large arrays live simultaneously before deserialization is rejected for exceeding the depth limit.

Because the array-header validation uses the total unread byte count as evidence that the declared elements may be present, nested array headers can reuse the same trailing bytes for this validation. This permits a relatively small payload to cause disproportionately large managed-heap allocations. The reported example uses an approximately 31.5 KiB payload to allocate roughly 114.7 MiB of reference storage on x64—an amplification factor of approximately 3,800—before the depth exception is raised. Repeated requests may cause severe memory pressure, excessive garbage collection, process termination, or loss of service availability.

Applications are affected when they:

  • Deserialize untrusted MessagePack data as object, or otherwise use a resolver path that selects PrimitiveObjectFormatter; and
  • Permit an attacker to submit such data repeatedly.

ASP.NET Core SignalR is one known way to expose the vulnerability remotely: an application that enables AddMessagePackProtocol() and has a reachable hub method with an object parameter may pass attacker-controlled arguments to the vulnerable MessagePack-CSharp formatter. However, the underlying vulnerability is in MessagePack-CSharp, not SignalR, and other applications that deserialize untrusted data through the same formatter may also be affected.

MessagePack-CSharp 2.5.302 is confirmed to contain the vulnerable code. Other releases containing the same allocate-before-depth-check behavior may also be affected. Authentication requirements depend on the application exposing the deserialization endpoint: exploitation requires no privileges for a publicly reachable endpoint, while protected endpoints retain their configured authorization requirements.

Workarounds

Where possible, avoid deserializing untrusted data into System.Object, including object-typed members of otherwise strongly typed models. Use concrete, narrowly defined DTO types instead.

For ASP.NET Core SignalR applications, any of the following can prevent or reduce exposure:

  • Replace object parameters in reachable hub methods with concrete types.
  • Disable the MessagePack hub protocol and use another protocol until a patched MessagePack-CSharp release is available.
  • Restrict affected hub methods to trusted and authenticated callers.
  • Apply rate limits and connection limits to reduce the ability to repeat malicious requests.

Reducing the maximum deserialization depth or transport message size may reduce the worst-case allocation, but should be treated only as defense in depth. It does not correct the allocate-before-depth-check behavior and is not a complete remediation.

Applications with advanced resolver configurations may use a custom formatter for object that enforces the depth limit before allocating arrays. Such a formatter should be carefully reviewed and tested against untrusted input.

items.content_html:
Impact

A small YAML OpenAPI document containing nested anchors and aliases can cause uncontrolled resource consumption in Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader and Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers. The issue affects OpenAPI document parsing through the public YAML reader APIs and can cause the parsing process to allocate excessive memory and terminate through out-of-memory conditions.

Affected versions

Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader

  • >= 2.0.0-preview.11, < 2.12.0
  • >= 3.0.0, < 3.10.0

Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers

  • < 1.6.30

Patches

  • For the 1.X major version, versions 1.6.30 and above are patched.
  • For the 2.X major version, versions 2.12.0 and above are patched.
  • For the 3.X major version, versions 3.10.0 and above are patched.

Impact

Applications, CLIs, developer tools, or services that parse untrusted YAML OpenAPI documents in-process may be terminated by a crafted YAML document containing nested anchors and aliases.

The impact is availability/process termination only. This report does not claim remote code execution, authentication bypass, credential exposure, privilege escalation, data exposure, or Microsoft hosted service impact.

Details

Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader and Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers parses YAML through SharpYaml. SharpYaml represents aliases as shared YamlNode instances in a directed acyclic graph, so the initial parsed YAML graph remains small. During conversion to System.Text.Json.Nodes.JsonNode, aliases must be materialized as independent nodes because JsonNode instances cannot be attached to multiple parents.

Without a bound on that conversion work, a small YAML document using nested anchors and aliases can expand exponentially during conversion. With N nested anchors each referenced k times, conversion can require k^N materialized JSON nodes, leading to excessive memory allocation and possible process termination.

This is an uncontrolled resource consumption vulnerability, also known as a "billion laughs" style denial of service.

Example payload

openapi: 3.0.0
info:
  title: Test
  version: 0.0.1
paths: {}
x-a: &a ["lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol", "lol"]
x-b: &b [*a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a, *a]
x-c: &c [*b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b, *b]
x-d: &d [*c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c, *c]
x-e: &e [*d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d, *d]
x-f: &f [*e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e, *e]

Remediation

Users should upgrade to Microsoft.OpenApi.YamlReader 2.12.0 or 3.10.0, or Microsoft.OpenApi.Readers 1.6.30, depending on the major version line they consume.

The patched versions bound YAML-to-JSON conversion work and fail fast instead of allowing unbounded expansion. The default limits are:

  • Maximum materialized node count: 5,000,000
  • Maximum nesting depth: 64

When the limits are exceeded, OpenApiYamlReader.Read reports an OpenApiDiagnostic error and does not return a parsed document.

The limits are exposed as process-wide static properties on YamlConverter for consumers that need to tune them for trusted workloads:

  • YamlConverter.MaxNodeCount
  • YamlConverter.MaxDepth

Applications that parse OpenAPI documents from untrusted sources should avoid parsing those documents in the primary application process when possible. Running parsing in an isolated process can reduce the blast radius of parser failures.

Executive summary

Microsoft is releasing this security advisory to provide information about a vulnerability in Microsoft.WindowsDesktop.App.Runtime (WPF). This advisory also provides guidance on what developers can do to update their applications to remove this vulnerability.

Restrictive XAML and XPS security fixes block unsafe URI fetching and navigation, propagate untrusted-input state through hyperlink navigation, add TrueType font protection and XAML nesting-depth limits, and avoid caching positive DNS zone-policy decisions.

Announcement

Announcement for this issue can be found at https://github.com/dotnet/announcements/issues/451

CVSS Details

  • Version: 3.1

  • Severity: High

  • Score: 8.8

  • Vector: CVSS:3.1/AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:R/S:U/C:H/I:H/A:H

  • Weakness: CWE-502 (Deserialization of Untrusted Data)

Affected Platforms

  • Platforms: Windows
  • Architectures: All

How do I know if I am affected?

If using a package listed in affected packages, you're exposed to the vulnerability.

How do I fix the issue?

  1. To fix the issue please install the latest version of .NET. If you have installed one or more .NET SDKs through Visual Studio, Visual Studio will prompt you to update Visual Studio, which will also update your .NET SDKs.
  2. If your application references the vulnerable package, update the package reference to the patched version. You can list the versions you have installed by running the dotnet --info command.

Once you have installed the updated runtime or SDK, restart your apps for the update to take effect.

Additionally, if you've deployed self-contained applications targeting any of the impacted versions, these applications are also vulnerable and must be recompiled and redeployed.
